mixture-composition-s1.title: Four samples at the particle level
mixture-composition-s1.html: Key: blue circle, nitrogen atom; orange circle, oxygen atom; small white circle, hydrogen atom; pink circle, argon atom.

mixture-composition-s2.title: How pure is a calcium supplement?
mixture-composition-s2.text: A calcium supplement tablet is calcium carbonate, CaCO₃ (100.09 g/mol), mixed with fillers that contain no calcium. A student analyzes three 1.250 g tablets from three brands for calcium.

table.caption: Mass of calcium found in each 1.250 g tablet

items.q: Which box shows a pure compound?
options: Box W
Box Y
Box X
Box Z

why.correct: A pure substance has one kind of particle. If those particles contain more than one element, it is a compound.
options: One kind of particle, but each has only nitrogen atoms: an element.
Three kinds of particles: a mixture.
Right: one kind of particle, and each particle contains two different elements.
Several kinds of particles: a mixture, even though it contains a compound.
Boxes Y and Z
Boxes W and Y
Boxes X and Z
Box Z by itself

why.correct: A mixture contains two or more substances, so its particles are not all alike. Y and Z qualify.
options: Right: each holds more than one kind of particle.
Box W has one kind of particle, so it is pure.
Box X has one kind of particle, so it is pure even though its molecules have two elements.
Box Y also holds three kinds of particles.

items.q: Box Y represents a sample of air. Why is air described as a mixture and not a compound?
options: It contains more than one element
It is a gas, and gases are mixtures
Each of its molecules contains one kind of atom
Its N₂, O₂ and Ar are separate, in proportions that can vary

why.correct: Air is several substances side by side, not one substance with a fixed formula. Its makeup (for example, its water vapor) can change from day to day.
options: A compound also contains more than one element; what matters is whether they form one kind of particle.
Some gases are pure, such as the nitrogen in Box W.
That describes each component, not why the whole sample is a mixture.
Right: the substances are not bonded into one kind of particle, and their amounts are not fixed.

items.q: In Box Y, what percentage of the particles are nitrogen molecules?

mistakes.why: Value: you counted atoms (8 N out of 13). The question asks for particles: 4 N₂ molecules out of 7.

why.correct: 4 N₂ out of 7 particles: 4/7 × 100 = 57.1%. The count of particles comes from the diagram, so this is a share by number, not by mass.

items.q: A student says Box Z is a pure compound because water is a compound. Which reply uses the particle diagram as evidence?
options: Box Z is not pure, because pure samples are solids
Box Z holds H₂O, O₂ and H₂: three kinds of particle
Box Z has an odd number of hydrogen atoms, so it is a mixture
Box Z is an element, since O₂ and H₂ are elements

why.correct: One kind of particle means pure; more than one means a mixture. Box Z shows three kinds.
options: Pure substances can be solids, liquids or gases.
Right: it cites what the diagram shows: three kinds of particles.
Atom counts do not decide this; the kinds of particles do.
Some of its particles are elements and some a compound; together they make a mixture.

items.q: What is the mass percent of calcium in pure CaCO₃? (Ca 40.08)
What is the percent purity (percent CaCO₃ by mass) of Brand P's tablet?

mistakes.why: Value: that is the percent calcium in the tablet. Convert the calcium to CaCO₃ first, then divide by the tablet mass.

items.q: Which brand's tablet contains the most filler?
options: Brand Q
Brand P
Brand R
The three have equal filler, since the tablets have equal masses

why.correct: Purity: P 90.0%, Q 99.0%, R 75.0%. The less calcium found, the less CaCO₃ and the more filler.
options: Brand Q has the most calcium, so the least filler.
Brand P has 10.0% filler, less than Brand R.
Right: least calcium, so least CaCO₃ (75.0%), so the most filler (25.0%).
Equal tablet masses, but different calcium contents, so different amounts of CaCO₃.

items.q: Suppose some of the filler in a tablet also contained calcium. How would the calculated purity compare with the true purity?
options: Too low, since the filler adds to the tablet's mass
Unchanged, since the CaCO₃ itself is weighed
Too high, since extra calcium is counted as CaCO₃
It could no longer be calculated from these data

why.correct: Elemental analysis is only as good as the assumption about where the element comes from. Calcium from the filler is wrongly counted as CaCO₃, so purity comes out too high.
options: The filler's mass is already in the tablet mass; the problem is the extra calcium.
The method weighs calcium, not CaCO₃, and assumes it all came from CaCO₃.
Right: the method assumes all Ca is in CaCO₃, so extra Ca inflates the CaCO₃ estimate.
It can be calculated; it would just be wrong in a predictable direction.

items.q: A label claims Brand Q is "99% pure calcium carbonate." Do the data support the claim?
options: Yes: 0.4955 g Ca is 1.237 g CaCO₃, 99.0% of 1.250 g
No: the tablet is 39.6% calcium, far below 99%
No: a 1.250 g tablet would need 1.24 g of calcium
Yes: the brands' tablets have equal masses, so equal purity
Right: the calculated purity matches the label.
Pure CaCO₃ is only 40.0% calcium, so 39.6% Ca is about 99% CaCO₃.
The claim is about calcium carbonate, not calcium; CaCO₃ is 40% Ca.
Equal masses say nothing about composition; Brand R is only 75.0% pure.
A bowl of cereal and milk
Pure water
Sand in water
Salt water, the same throughout

why.correct: A homogeneous mixture has the same composition throughout; a heterogeneous one has visibly different regions.
options: You can see separate parts, so it is heterogeneous.
Pure water is a single substance, not a mixture.
The sand settles into a visibly different layer: heterogeneous.
Right: the composition is uniform, so it is homogeneous.

items.q: Two samples of a gray powder are both iron and sulfur. Sample 1 is 63.5% Fe by mass every time it is tested. Sample 2 is 30% Fe in one scoop and 55% Fe in another. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Both are mixtures, because both contain two elements
Sample 1 is likely a compound; Sample 2, an uneven mixture
Both are compounds, because both contain iron and sulfur
Sample 2 is likely a compound because its iron content is lower

why.correct: A compound has a fixed composition (FeS is 63.5% Fe). A mixture's composition can vary, and if it varies within one sample, the mixture is heterogeneous.
options: Compounds contain two or more elements too; fixed vs varying composition is what tells them apart.
Right: fixed composition points to a compound; composition that varies between scoops points to an uneven mixture.
A compound has one fixed composition; Sample 2 varies from scoop to scoop.
The size of the percent does not decide it; whether it stays fixed does.

items.q: A 5.00 g mixture of table salt (NaCl, 60.66% Cl by mass) and sugar (no chlorine) contains 1.515 g of chlorine. What mass of salt is in the mixture?

mistakes.why: Value: you multiplied by the fraction. The salt is the whole and chlorine the part, so divide by 0.6066.
Value: that assumes the whole mixture is salt. Only the salt holds chlorine.

why.correct: All the chlorine is in the salt: 1.515 g Cl ÷ 0.6066 = 2.498 g NaCl.

items.q: Which observations are at the macroscopic level? Select all that apply.
options: The solid is shiny and gray
The sample has a mass of 2.48 g
Each particle holds one Fe and one S atom
Oxygen molecules are made of two atoms

why.correct: Macroscopic means observable or measurable in bulk; the particle level describes atoms and molecules.
options: Right: something you can see.
Right: measured on a balance.
That is the particle level.
That is the particle level.

items.q: A student adds more sugar to a 5.00 g mixture of salt and sugar. Predict how each quantity changes.

variables.name: Mass of chlorine in the sample
variables.why: Only the salt holds chlorine, and no salt was added.

variables.name: Mass percent of chlorine in the sample
variables.why: The same chlorine is now spread over a larger total mass.

variables.name: Mass percent of chlorine in the salt itself
variables.why: NaCl is a compound with a fixed composition, 60.66% Cl.

why.correct: Adding one part of a mixture changes the mixture's composition, not the composition of the compounds in it.

items.q: A student wants to know if a sample of baking soda is pure. Which measurement would best test this?
options: Measure the mass of the sample very carefully
Look at it closely to check that it is evenly white
Compare its mass percent of sodium with the pure compound's
Count the particles in a drawing of the sample

why.correct: Elemental analysis compares a measured mass percent with the fixed value for the pure compound. A mismatch means the sample is a mixture.
options: The mass alone says nothing about what the sample is made of.
Many white powders could be mixed in without any change in color.
Right: a pure compound has a fixed mass percent of each element; a mixture would differ.
A drawing is a model; you need a measurement of the real sample.
